carFree.title: Can you live in {city} without a car?
carFree.verdictEasy: Yes — {city} scores {score}/100 on our car-free score, so commuting, errands and nights out all work on foot or by public transport. Most residents here can skip car ownership entirely, and the savings go straight into the rest of the budget.
carFree.verdictDoable: Mostly — at {score}/100, {city} handles everyday trips on foot and by public transport, but a car still helps for weekend trips, bulk shopping and anything outside the built-up core.
carFree.verdictMixed: Partly — {city} scores {score}/100. Central neighbourhoods work without a car, but move out to the cheaper suburbs and you will want one for commuting and shopping. Budget for a car, or pay the centre's rent premium.
carFree.verdictCarNeeded: Not easily — at {score}/100, {city} is built around driving. Plan for a car and its running costs, or expect long trips and a narrow choice of neighbourhoods.
carFree.transportBelow: Transport in {city} indexes at {index} against a US average of 100 — about {pct}% cheaper than a typical US city. That line covers fares, fuel and running a vehicle, so it is the one that moves most when you drop the car.
carFree.transportAbove: Transport in {city} indexes at {index} against a US average of 100 — about {pct}% more expensive than a typical US city. That line covers fares, fuel and running a vehicle, so it is the one that moves most when you drop the car.
carFree.transportEqual: Transport in {city} indexes at {index}, level with the US average. That line covers fares, fuel and running a vehicle, so it is the one that moves most when you drop the car.

carFree.note: The car-free score is our own composite: 60% walkability, 40% public transport, both on a 0–100 scale. Like the rest of our quality-of-life figures, they are calibrated estimates, not official statistics.

affordability.title: Is {city} expensive?
affordability.verdictVeryExpensive: Yes — {city} is one of the expensive ones. Its cost-of-living index is {index} against a US average of 100, so a month here runs about {pct}% more than in a typical US city. Housing does most of that damage; the rest of the basket follows it up.
affordability.verdictExpensive: Yes, moderately. {city} indexes at {index} against a US average of 100 — roughly {pct}% above it. That is above average without being in the top bracket, and which neighbourhood you rent in decides most of the gap.
affordability.verdictModerate: Not really — {city} indexes at {index} against a US average of 100, so a month here lands within a few percent of a typical US city. Expect the surprises in individual lines rather than in the total.
affordability.verdictAffordable: No — {city} indexes at {index} against a US average of 100, about {pct}% below it. Rent is the line that moves most, and a US or Western European salary stretches noticeably further here.
affordability.verdictCheap: No — {city} is one of the cheap ones, indexing at {index} against a US average of 100: roughly {pct}% below a typical US city. The trade-offs usually show up in local wages, healthcare or infrastructure rather than in prices.

Your own total moves with the neighbourhood, your habits and whether you run a car.

why.lead: Moving city or country is one of the biggest money decisions you will make — and most cost-of-living figures online are guesses. walkableExplainer: Walkability decides more of your budget than it looks. Where errands, work and school are a walk or a short tram ride away, a car is optional — and dropping it removes a payment, insurance, fuel, parking and maintenance from the monthly total. In a car-dependent city that same money is simply part of the cost of living, whatever the rent looks like.

The score below runs 0–100 and answers one question: how much of everyday life can you reach on foot? Dense, mixed-use centres with short blocks and shops at street level score high; cities where housing, work and shopping sit in separate zones score low. Public transport is scored separately, so a city can be walkable in its core and still have thin transit — or the reverse.

Every city page pairs the two into a car-free score and says whether living without a car there is realistic, alongside that city's transport cost index (US average = 100). Read it together with rent: the cheap suburb stops being cheap once it needs a car, and a pricier walkable centre can come out ahead.
